articles.title: Caring for Children
articles.author: Colin Greer, Reynard Loki
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Children form their understanding of society through the people around them: the person who greets them at the classroom door, the coach who notices when something’s wrong, the nurse who explains a scary procedure gently, the librarian who saves a book, the neighbor who walks them home. Policy, institutions, and cultural norms—the subjects of the first five articles in this series—often reach children through these adults. A well-funded program or a well-written law can change a child’s circumstances. articles.title: National Security Has Failed
articles.author: Lawrence S. Wittner
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For millennia, the world’s people have been kidding themselves about national security. Worried about the survival of their nation in a world of self-interested, sometimes aggressive nations, people have armed and prepared themselves for war. Only military strength, they have assumed, would fend off or defeat a military attack on their nation. And a case can be made for this assumption, for not all nations–and not all people–are willing to deal peacefully or justly with their neighbors. articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content_excerpt: After months of organizing that began early in the summer, the UAW is on track to knock more than 300,000 doors with UAW members and union households as part of its biggest electoral program in decades. The UAW is using its membership-focused political program, modeled on the success of the 2023 Stand Up Strike, to reach working-class voters from UAW households in key Senate and House races nationwide. In several key districts where UAW membership exceeds the previous election’s margin of victory, the UAW has more than 130 full-time political organizers in the field and has mobilized thousands of volunteers. articles.content_excerpt: Between all the action around next week’s midterms and Donald Trump’s meddling in Brazilian politics, it’s easy to forget there’s a war going on. articles.title: Preparing for MAGA’s Worst on Election Day
articles.author: Stephanie Luce
articles.content_excerpt: Imagine this: Election Day comes and goes. Democrats turn out big and flip a few seats, some by close margins. Forces opposing the increasingly authoritarian drift of the United States breathe a sigh of relief. Before the results are even called, however, Donald Trump declares in a wave of Truth Social posts that Democrats have cheated, the results are fraudulent, and those responsible will be prosecuted and persecuted. By the next day, the claims have spread to congressional Republicans, who vow to seek justice — and, in some cases, vengeance — for the supposed voter fraud. articles.title: Dolores Huerta Taught a Generation How to Organize
articles.author: David Bacon
articles.content_excerpt: When I came back from a solidarity work brigade in Cuba in the 1970s, I landed in New York City with no place to sleep. I called Lori Huerta, a friend from California, and daughter of Dolores Huerta (1930–2026), cofounder of the United Farm Workers (UFW). Not only did I get space on the floor of the NYC grape boycott headquarters, but Dolores and her partner, Richard, César Chávez’s brother, took us out to eat. Over pizza I enthused about the island. I had stars in my eyes, for both Cuba and Dolores, and still do. I went to work for the UFW as an organizer a few months later. At the beginning of the Iraq War, Huerta marches with actor Danny Glover and an enormous crowd demanding that the troops be brought home. articles.title: Where Did Black Los Angeles Go? The Disappearance of a Community That Built the City
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Part Two of Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? Los Angeles celebrates its diversity. Its leaders routinely invoke the contributions of the many communities that have shaped the city. But something extraordinary has happened to one of those communities. Black Los Angeles has been disappearing. In 1980, approximately 496,000 Black people lived in Los Angeles, representing nearly 17 percent of its population. By 2020, that number had fallen to approximately 367,000, or about 9 percent. The city lost more than one-quarter of its Black population even as its overall population grew. articles.title: Minneapolis Refused to Take Trump’s Bait. It Paid Off.
articles.author: Eric Blanc
articles.content_excerpt: All signs point toward a resounding rebuke of Donald Trump in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Democrats have opened up a commanding lead in national polls , Trump’s popularity has sunk to historic lows, and even many of his former supporters are turning against him. There are plenty of reasons for this collapse, from rising prices to Trump’s disastrous war with Iran. But we shouldn’t forget what was arguably the single most important turning point of his presidency: the defeat of his militarized assault on Minneapolis. In January, Trump’s administration set out to terrorize immigrants, crush resistance, and establish the precedent that federal forces could occupy American cities against the wishes of their residents and elected officials. articles.title: Socialists Need Our Own Foreign Policy Agenda
articles.author: Max B. Sawicky
articles.content_excerpt: It is common for mainstream news outlets and political commentators in the United States to describe socialists as “very liberal” or simply “progressive,” or to puzzle over how to draw ideological lines between democratic socialists and others on the broad Left. There are, in fact, serious differences — differences that socialists would do well to sharpen and articulate for the public. At the same time, as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) grows by leaps and bounds, some commentators prefer to highlight those DSA positions that are furthest from common agreement. I have previously tried to distinguish between socialists and liberals when it comes to domestic economic policy. But what about foreign policy? Here I propose a socialist agenda for this field.
